cards.concept: Why must BM25 saturate term frequency?
cards.intuition: The first occurrence is strong evidence of aboutness, while each repetition adds less. A bounded curve prevents keyword stuffing from buying unlimited score.
cards.topic: Term Frequency Saturation: The Role of k1

cards.intuition: k1 is the term frequency at which the simple saturation curve reaches half its ceiling. Smaller values make presence dominate; larger values let repetition matter longer.
cards.formula: k1 = 0 gives binary behavior; very large k1 approaches linear tf behavior
cards.topic: Term Frequency Saturation: The Role of k1

cards.concept: Why does production BM25 multiply by k1 + 1?
cards.intuition: The factor rescales every term curve so one occurrence in an average-length document contributes exactly one unit of tf weight. It changes scale, not ranking.
cards.topic: Term Frequency Saturation: The Role of k1

cards.intuition: A long document may repeat the same ideas wordily or may honestly cover more topics. Length normalization penalizes the first explanation, while too much of it harms the second.
cards.formula: b chooses the blend between no normalization and full length normalization
cards.topic: Length Normalization: The Role of b

cards.intuition: Compare a document with the collection average, then blend that ratio with one. Short documents get an effective tf boost and long documents need more occurrences for equal evidence.
cards.topic: Length Normalization: The Role of b

cards.intuition: At zero, all document lengths are treated alike. At one, term frequency is fully normalized by relative document length. Intermediate values hedge between scope and verbosity.
cards.topic: Length Normalization: The Role of b

cards.intuition: For each matched query term, multiply rarity by a bounded term-frequency signal adjusted for document length, then add the term contributions. Inverted postings make the matched-term sum efficient.
cards.formula: BM25(q,d) = sum over matched t of idf(t) × tf(t,d)(k1+1) / [tf(t,d) + k1((1-b)+b|d|/avgdl)]

cards.concept: What evidence does BM25 not model?
cards.intuition: Matched terms get strong lexical scoring, but term proximity, synonymy, and semantic equivalence are absent. This is why dense retrieval complements rather than merely duplicates BM25.
cards.formula: BM25 has no built-in proximity or semantic matching

cards.concept: How do k1 and b decide winners?
cards.intuition: k1 controls how much repeated mentions help, while b controls how strongly length discounts them. A shorter document can beat a longer one with more raw occurrences when both effects are strong.
cards.formula: higher k1 rewards sustained repetition; higher b penalizes long documents more

cards.intuition: Raise b when rambling pages dominate and lower it when comprehensive documents lose to stubs. Lower k1 for keyword stuffing and raise it when one-off mentions beat sustained coverage.
cards.formula: tune k1 and b against representative judged queries and the product metric
cards.topic: Tuning k1 and b in Practice

cards.concept: Why must BM25 be retuned after corpus changes?
cards.intuition: Chunking, analyzers, and fields alter document lengths and term frequencies, which are the statistics BM25 uses. Constants tuned for the old distribution may encode the wrong tradeoff.
cards.formula: revalidate after changes to chunking, fields, analyzers, or query mix
cards.topic: Tuning k1 and b in Practice

cards.intuition: Classical RSJ idf becomes negative above fifty-percent document frequency. Lucene adds one inside the logarithm to keep common-term weights positive.
cards.topic: Tuning k1 and b in Practice

cards.concept: Why use rank fusion for BM25 and dense scores?
cards.intuition: BM25 depends on collection statistics while cosine similarity lives on a different scale. Rank fusion discards incomparable raw magnitudes and combines ordering instead.
cards.formula: BM25 scores are not comparable across collections or directly to cosine scores
cards.topic: Tuning k1 and b in Practice
